articles.title: 3 UP youths missing in Russia; told kin ‘forced to fight against Ukraine’
articles.summary: Three youths from western UP missing in Moscow after last calls; families say passports seized and they were forced into Russian army. MEA, embassy seek details.
articles.body: AGRA/SHAMLI: Amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict, families of three young men from western Uttar Pradesh are living in despair after losing contact with their sons in Moscow.The youths, who travelled to Russia on study visas last year, reportedly claimed before going silent that local authorities confiscated their passports and forced them into military service.The missing youths are Himanshu Sharma (24) and Shakti Punder (23), both from Muzaffarnagar, and Ashu Saini (25) from Shamli district. The three men were sharing a room in the Russian capital Moscow and were pursuing a Russian language course.According to relatives, the last contact with the students came on July 30, when brief phone calls were made before their lines went dead and their phones switched off. Himanshu Sharma went to Russia on a student visa to study and take up permissible part-time work.His cousin, Priyanshu Sharma, told reporters, “His passport was due to expire this year. Since that last call on July 30, we have called his number several times with no response. We suspect he could be forced into the Russian Army.”Similarly, Shakti Punder’s father reported speaking to him last on the same day, after which all communication ceased.Ashu Saini hailed from Hasanpur Lohari village in Shamli’s Thanabhawan area and left for Russia in April 2026. His sister, Anshul, recalled a hurried 30-second final conversation where he briefly mentioned he was fine before hanging up.Ashu’s father, Rakesh Kumar, a farmer, has formally appealed to the Prime Minister’s Office seeking his son’s safe return.Following desperate pleas from the families, appeals were dispatched to ministry of external affairs (MEA). In response, MEA informed the families that India’s embassy in Moscow has actively intervened.“The embassy has taken up the matter with the Russian authorities concerned. They have reportedly joined the Russian army; the embassy has sought details of their whereabouts. The embassy is separately taking up their case,” the MEA stated in its reply to the families of the youths.In July, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal acknowledged that approximately 24 Indian citizens—recruited through fraudulent or non-transparent means—remain stuck serving within the ranks of Russian army as the war in Ukraine persists.While local authorities in Uttar Pradesh have assured grieving families that inquiries are underway and assistance will be extended, relatives continue to wait anxiously for their safe repatriation.(With inputs from Sudeep Lavania in Agra and Sachin Sharma in Shamli)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Agra | Silver Rate in Agra | Bank Holidays in Agra | Public Holidays in Agra | Agra AQI | Weather in Agra | Petrol Price in Agra | Diesel Price in Agra | CNG Price in Agra | LPG Price in AgraStay updated with the latest Agra news. articles.title: Yellowstone National Park retrieved 280 hats from hydrothermal vents this summer
articles.summary: Other lost items include hair ties, dozens of lens caps, AirPods, and even an inhaler.
articles.body:
Yellowstone National Park attracts more than 4.5 million visitors from around the world every year. Many sightseers arrive well prepared to admire the hotsprings, geysers , scenic lookouts , and wildlife , but there is only so much anyone can do about life's little unexpected accidents. Each season, Yellowstone's gusty winds are responsible for blowing away hundreds of hats, maps, and even sunglasses from the heads and hands of onlookers. And every season, park workers scour the grounds to gather up any lost items that landed far from the walkways and trails.

While the tally so far isn't quite as large as last year's haul , Yellowstone officials still impressively retrieved more than 280 hats from the hydrothermal areas. Workers cited standouts including a FIFA 2026 Men's World Cup souvenir and a baseball cap ironically emblazoned with "Cowboy Hat." But just because they aren't suited for floating around roiling geysers doesn't mean they're destined for a landfill. Once the 2026 season draws to a close, all of the collected hats will be cleaned and donated to local clothing organizations.

Caps are only one type of lost item located amid the hunts. Workers scooped up more than $18 in coins from around the world during the summer search. Canadian dollars, euros, pesos, and yen were scattered among the U.S. change, many apparently tossed into hot springs and geysers as if they were wishing wells. Yellowstone officials took the occasion to remind everyone that hydrothermal formations are not made to receive wished-upon coins. Not only will your dream remain unfulfilled—the foreign additions often introduce destructive algae and bacteria into the delicate ecosystems.

Other common detritus in the haul included plenty of paper and plastic trash, hair ties, hotel key cards, children's toys, eyewear, and camera lens caps. Standout oddities such as AirPods, an inhaler, and even a single Uno card also made the list of finds.

As always, Yellowstone workers reminded everyone that the seasonal roundup also serves as an excellent reminder to "stash your trash." Visitors are encouraged to place any litter or lightweight items deep in their pockets or bags until they reach a trash can. And although headwear is always important protection from the sun, people may want to consider temporarily removing their hats while trekking through especially windy areas of the park.

articles.title: Why cash continues to thrive even as India's digital payments grow
articles.summary: Digital payments are booming, yet cash remains deeply embedded in the economy in India, central bank data shows.
articles.body:
Every year, more Indians tap, scan and swipe. Every year they also hoard more paper.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) - the country's central bank - now has 176 billion banknotes in circulation. It's printing 28-30 billion fresh ones across six denominations annually and retiring roughly 21 billion. It is a vast logistics operation.

And yet, as Unified Payments Interface (UPI) digital transactions surge towards a billion a day, cash sloshing around the economy keeps climbing at a brisk pace.

"Currency in circulation continues to grow at double-digit rates even as cash's share of individual transactions declines, thanks to growing digital payment adoption. That combination makes future demand harder to predict, which complicates our planning for production and distribution capacity," Shirish Chandra Murmu, RBI deputy governor, said in a speech to central bankers in Jakarta last month.

He called it the "cash paradox". But what exactly do we mean by currency in circulation?

It is the total value of physical banknotes and coins held by the public and businesses, whether spent or simply held. In India, cash reaches them through four main channels: the RBI's 19 regional offices; bank branches; more than 250,000 ATMs and cash dispensers; and millions of "business correspondents", local agents who provide basic banking services in rural areas and smaller towns.

That is a huge stock of cash by any measure. For context, about 56 billion US dollar bills and 30 billion euro banknotes were in circulation at the end of last year, according to Murmu.

The comparison comes with a caveat: the RBI's count is partly driven by a higher share of lower-value notes, meaning more notes are needed to handle the same value of transactions.

The puzzle is not that Indians still use cash - 94% of transactions were cash-based as recently as 2019, according to new research by Anirudh Tagat, Mehmet Ozmen and Pushpa Trivedi. It is that cash is growing even as its share of everyday payments shrinks.

"The cash paradox has been examined globally, and India is a unique and novel case study of the same given the scale of both cash and non-cash payments," Tagat, an economist who studies Indian payment behaviour, told the BBC.

He notes that the phenomenon of cash growing alongside digital payments has been especially prominent since the 2007-08 global financial crisis, with Bank for International Settlements research showing a similar pattern worldwide.

In Tagat's framing, currency still serves three purposes - as a means of payment, a store of value and a hedge against calamity. Apps are replacing only the first. That helps explain why digital payments alone cannot tell the whole story of cash demand.

David Humphrey of Florida State University, who has studied cash use across 14 economies with co-author Tanai Khiaonarong, says digital payment adoption is just one of several factors that can influence how much cash people hold.

That raises another question: are households holding more cash outside the banking system - for emergencies, safekeeping or to buy assets such as gold in India?

He also points to a factor that is especially important for major reserve currencies: a lot of the growth comes from notes held or used abroad, rather than in the country that issued them.

The US is a case in point: large-denomination $50 and $100 notes are widely held and used overseas but are "rarely seen in normal domestic legal cash transactions", Humphrey says.

He add that the Federal Reserve regularly receives unfit US currency from abroad, replaces it with fit notes and returns them to the sender. Most of the value of these unfit notes is in $50 and $100 bills.

This helps explain, he says, why the Fed reports that the total value of US currency in circulation continues to rise even as the value of cash withdrawn from domestic ATMs - a proxy for everyday spending, mostly in $20 notes, along with $5 and $10 bills - has recently fallen.

Then there is the less visible side of the cash economy. Humphrey's research identifies the rising value of domestic illegal activity, which often relies on unrecorded cash transactions, as one structural reason currency growth can outpace recorded spending - a factor particularly relevant to India.

Property deals in India routinely involve cash payments, partly because stamp duty and government-set "circle rates" can lag market prices, giving buyers and sellers an incentive to under-declare the transaction and settle the difference in cash.

Demonetisation , which overnight invalidated 86% of the country's cash by value in 2016, attacked the stock of "black" cash but left this flow largely untouched, say economists. That helps explain why decades of estimates of "black money" sunk into real estate have never produced a reliable figure.

Then there is what might be called the psychology of frictionlessness. Tagat points to research, including work published recently in the Journal of Consumer Research, showing digital payments are increasingly engineered to strip out the "pain" of paying - the wince of handing over notes - and replace it with a satisfying beep.

That should, in theory, hollow out cash demand further. That it has not suggests something else is propping currency up: fear - not just the fear of spending, but the fear of what happens when digital systems fail.

Here the Indian story rhymes with Europe's.

The European Central Bank (ECB) has watched euro banknotes in circulation rise from about €1 trillion in 2016 to €1.6 trillion this year, even as cash's share of point-of-sale transactions has fallen towards half.

Philip Lane, the ECB's chief economist, told a summer conference in Ireland this year that while the number of notes used in transactions is falling, the stock held by households keeps growing - something identical to what Murmu alluded to in Jakarta.

Olive McCarthy, a professor at University College Cork, traces this to the ECB's own 2021 research on what it dubbed the "paradox of banknotes", driven by households hoarding cash as savings and by demand for euros outside the currency zone itself.

Governments in Austria, Finland , Germany , Sweden and the Netherlands have responded by formally advising citizens to keep a minimum amount of cash at home, insurance against blackouts, cyberattacks or war. Clearly, cash, in rich democracies as much as in India, is being repositioned as critical infrastructure for bad days rather than good ones.

McCarthy lists who depends on it most bluntly: the elderly, the rural poor, domestic-violence victims hiding transactions from an abuser, and children learning what money is. "Some consumers," she told me, "prefer the privacy and convenience of cash."

For India's RBI, this creates an awkward budgeting problem.

It runs its own paper mills, four currency printing presses and ink plants - an entire supply chain built for self-reliance - while promoting the world's most successful instant-payments network.

Tagat says this creates a difficult choice for the RBI: how much to invest in managing cash and how much in promoting digital payments, especially as trials of 10 and 20 rupee polymer notes - first proposed a decade ago - finally get under way. (Polymer notes are more durable than paper ones, potentially reducing the cost and frequency of replacing worn-out cash.)

Murmu framed reliable cash as part of "monetary sovereignty". Tagat says the rupee's informal use across South Asia gives India another reason to keep its currency machinery running, as a shock-absorber for the whole region.

"The RBI," Tagat says, "has a strong case for keeping cash going despite new digital payments alternatives."

If UPI, as reported, starts attracting transaction charges on smaller payments, cash may claw back share even in the payments column, not just the savings one, he adds.

The lesson for policymakers is clear, and mildly humbling: digital payments have not made cash obsolete. Cash is less a technology being replaced than an insurance policy nobody wants to give up.

articles.title: On Shah's UCC claim, 3 BJP allies sound caution
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A day after Union home minister Amit Shah expressed confidence that 21 NDA-governed states would implement Uniform Civil Code by 2029, thre.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A day after Union home minister Amit Shah expressed confidence that 21 NDA-governed states would implement Uniform Civil Code by 2029, three BJP allies struck a circumspect note.Lavu Sri Krishna Devarayalu, parliamentary party leader of Telugu Desam Party which is in office in Andhra Pradesh, told TOI, "As of now, there is no discussion but whenever we find the need for it, we will look into it. We will definitely involve various stakeholders before we adopt it."JD(U), which is part of the BJP-led coalition in Bihar, said it would speak with Shah. "I will meet home minister Amit Shah and discuss the issue," the party's working president Sanjay Jha told TOI.JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar, who stepped down as Bihar's longest-serving CM to make way for BJP's Samrat Chaudhary in April, had in the past supported the idea of UCC but emphasised that a consensus should be evolved by taking all communities on board.Another BJP ally, Chirag Paswan of Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), also chose to be cautious, saying his party was committed to uniformity and diversity and the Constitution has acknowledged different traditions and practices of different communities. Exemptions for Scheduled Tribes under different schedules and articles of the Constitution were proof of this, he said.The proposal for UCC should be made public, interests of stakeholders considered and comprehensive consultation should follow, he said, adding that his party would make its stand clear after this.JDU, TDP have history of independent positionsBoth Telugu Desam Party and JD(U) have a history of taking independent positions on some of the key ideological planks of the BJP since 2014. Both have been in and out of the NDA during this period but are seen to be aligned more closely with the BJP in the third term of PM Narendra Modi. Despite being a BJP ally, JD(U) MPs had not voted in support of Article 370’s abrogation in Parliament in 2019 and had walked out.Addressing a press conference in Mumbai, Shah had said, “Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced Uniform Civil Code in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce UCC before 2029.”The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.BJP has gone for the rollout of UCC through states governed by it instead of its nationwide implementation in one go. It is already in force in Uttarakhand, while Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh have passed the law as well.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body:
The Guardian and the Times lead on the government's plans to introduce stricter residency checks for people donating to political parties – a move that could block the £72m given to Reform UK by two cryptocurrency tycoons.

A source tells the Times that potential donors might have to prove that they've lived in the UK for at least 183 days a year.

In a separate article the paper says Reform is already spending the money, it's doubling its policy team from 10 to 20, recruiting 400 field agents and preparing its YouTube channel.

In an editorial the Daily Mail accuses Labour of "hyperventilating hypocrisy".

The paper says there's nothing to prove that the two tycoons are seeking to benefit from their gifts to Reform, whereas Labour depends on funding from trade unions and it rewards them with changes to legislation that favour their members.

The Daily Mirror says the Reform leader, Nigel Farage can rail against the rules and attack the establishment as much as he likes. The paper says "the floundering leader propped up by two billionaires" cannot expect voters to stop asking whose interests his party would really serve in power.

The village of Piddington in Oxfordshire, where people are protesting against a plan to build a camp for asylum seekers, is on the front pages of the Daily Express and Daily Telegraph . The Express says the campaign group Women of Piddington has written about security fears to all 266 female MPs, but only four have responded.

The i Paper says a review commissioned by the government will say that ADHD is not being widely overdiagnosed.

However, the report – to be published within weeks – will say that record numbers of people are seeking an official diagnosis in order to access support and benefits.

According to the Financial Times , France has stunned other EU countries with a request to remove the Russian-Uzbek oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the list of people and organisations targeted by European sanctions. The paper says France's move is linked to its efforts to secure the release of a number of French citizens imprisoned in Azerbaijan.

And finally, the Telegraph reports that Halloween pumpkins will be too small to carve this year, after drought damaged their growth. Farmers say they'll be about 40% smaller than usual.

articles.title: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
articles.summary: The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.
articles.body:
The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

It is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published, the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons that cap would be £100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK. Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.

Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address? Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?

The Communities Minister Baroness Taylor told the Lords that Brits returning from abroad and wanting to donate without limit "must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom" and the government is "considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy".

In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.

Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.

Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?

The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.

Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.

Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'

Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall

Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?

Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo?

So, there are loads of questions that tumble towards us after these donations.

Should there be a limit on the proportion of a party's funding that can come from one individual?

Should there be a limit on what donors based in the UK can give per year, as well as a cap on donations from Brits abroad?

The General Secretary of the Unite union has suggested a domestic cap somewhere between £500,000 and £1m a year. Some argue this would compel parties to find their funding via lots of small donations rather than fewer giant ones. But it could also prompt some to call for state funding of political parties – ie taxpayers picking up the tab – which may not prove wildly popular.

Then there is the question of spending limits, in addition to donation limits, between elections on the top of the existing limits that do apply just before elections.

If I am leaving you with the impression that these donations to Reform, and in particular their scale, are transforming the debates at Westminster about politics and money, well - they are.

And yes, all of the political parties are aware of their own narrow, self interest in all of this - as well as their own sense of the wider good.

articles.title: Círio de Nazaré 2026: Belém espera 105 mil turistas e R$ 207 milhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Estimativa é do Observatório do Turismo do Pará e do Dieese/PA. Número representa um crescimento de 5% em relação ao ano passado, quando a festa atraiu cerca de 100 mil visitantes.
articles.summary: Estimativa do Dieese aponta que o Círio de Nazaré 2026 atrairá 105 mil turistas, injetando R$ 207 milhões na economia e no turismo em Belém.
articles.body:
O Círio de Nazaré de 2026, que será realizado no dia 11 de outubro, deve atrair cerca de 105 mil turistas a Belém . A estimativa é do Observatório do Turismo do Pará, em parceria com o Departamento Intersindical de Estatística e Estudos Socioeconômicos (Dieese/PA).

O número representa um crescimento de 5% em relação a 2025, quando a festa recebeu cerca de 100 mil visitantes.

Os gastos dos turistas também devem aumentar. A projeção para este ano é de cerca de US$ 40,6 milhões, contra US$ 38,9 milhões em 2025, um crescimento de 4,4%. Usando o dólar comercial a R$ 5,112, cotação do dia nove de setembro, o valor equivale a aproximadamente R$ 207,5 milhões. Pel o mesmo câmbio, os gastos de 2025 chegaram a R$ 198,9 milhões.

Círio de Nazaré reúne mais de 2,6 milhões de pessoas em Belém. — Foto: Nicksson Melo / g1 Pará

Os dados vêm de uma pesquisa feita com 1.200 turistas entre 8 e 15 de outubro de 2025, em locais próximos ao Centro Arquitetônico de Nazaré, à Basílica e à Casa de Plácido. O levantamento foi aplicado pela Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA).

A maioria dos visitantes é mulher (52,75%) e tem entre 35 e 50 anos (35,33%). Depois aparecem as faixas de 51 a 65 anos (24,92%) e de 26 a 34 anos (21,83%). O nível de escolaridade é alto: 42,50% têm ensino superior completo e 25,67% têm pós-graduação.

As rendas mais comuns ficam entre dois e três salários mínimos (24,83%) e entre quatro e cinco salários mínimos (24,17%). O Maranhão é o estado que mais envia turistas, seguido por São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Ceará e Amazonas. A pesquisa também identificou visitantes de todas as outras unidades da federação.

A viagem é, em boa parte, em família: 50,75% dos entrevistados vieram com parentes, 27,17% em grupo e 22,08% sozinhos. A grande maioria (86,42%) não comprou pacote turístico.

O avião foi o meio de transporte mais usado (60,67%). Carro próprio e ônibus de empresa empataram, com 12,33% cada.

Na hospedagem, a casa de parentes foi a opção mais citada (38,08%), seguida por hotéis (26,33%) e casas de amigos (15,08%). Quase seis em cada dez turistas (59,22%) ficaram em Belém entre três e sete dias. A permanência média fica em torno de sete dias.

Durante a estadia, 31,17% disseram que pretendiam conhecer outras localidades. Os destinos mais citados foram Salinópolis, Mosqueiro, Marajó, Bragança e Combu. Na capital, os pontos mais lembrados são a Basílica de Nazaré, a Estação das Docas, o Ver-o-Peso, o Porto Futuro e o Mangal das Garças.

A festa tem forte poder de fidelização: 63,83% dos turistas já haviam participado do Círio antes, e 93% pretendem voltar. A principal forma de conhecer a festa é o boca a boca — amigos ou parentes responderam por 67% das respostas, bem à frente da internet e das redes sociais (10,50%) e da TV e do rádio (8,33%).

Entre os pontos positivos de Belém, os turistas destacaram a gastronomia (23,00%), a hospitalidade (19,50%), a cultura (6,42%), os pontos turísticos (6,17%) e a beleza da cidade (4,42%).

Já o que precisa melhorar, na visão deles, é o trânsito (22,17%), a limpeza urbana (12,75%), a segurança (4,75%) e o transporte (3,42%).

Na pesquisa de 2025, a alimentação foi o item que mais consumiu o orçamento dos visitantes: 38,14% dos gastos. Depois vêm hospedagem (28,62%), lembranças e souvenires (18,13%) e transporte interno (15,11%).

O gasto médio por dia foi de R$ 150,11, e o gasto médio individual, de cerca de R$ 960,11.

Segundo o Observatório do Turismo e o Dieese/PA, o impacto do Círio vai além dos dias de procissão. O evento envolve preparação, deslocamentos e consumo em vários setores, movimentando desde grandes empresas até pequenos negócios, trabalhadores autônomos e a economia popular.

Para as instituições, os resultados também apontam prioridades: melhorar trânsito, limpeza, segurança e transporte, ampliar a divulgação e estimular a visita a outros destinos paraenses são medidas que podem fazer os turistas ficarem mais tempo e espalhar melhor os ganhos do turismo pelo estado.

articles.body:
A Lotofácil da Independência 2026 será sorteada nesta terça-feira (15), a partir das 21h. O concurso especial, de número 3780, tem prêmio estimado em R$ 300 milhões .

Anteriormente o sorteio estava programado para às 11h, no entanto, foi adiado pela Caixa.

Uma das particularidades da Lotofácil da Independência é que o prêmio principal não acumula. Se não houver ganhador na faixa dos 15 números, o valor destinado a essa faixa é distribuído entre os ganhadores da faixa seguinte, de acordo com as regras da modalidade.

As apostas podem ser registradas até as 18h desta terça-feira (15).

Para participar, o apostador precisa escolher entre 15 e 20 números, dentre os 25 disponíveis no volante da Lotofácil. A aposta simples, com 15 dezenas, custa R$ 3,50.

É possível fazer o jogo nas lotéricas, pelo portal Loterias Caixa ou pelo aplicativo Loterias Caixa. Também estão disponíveis opções como Surpresinha, quando os números são escolhidos aleatoriamente pelo sistema, e Teimosinha.

O prêmio da Lotofácil da Independência acumula?

Não . Uma das principais características da Lotofácil da Independência é que o prêmio principal não acumula.

Caso não haja nenhuma aposta com os 15 números sorteados, o valor destinado à faixa principal é distribuído entre os ganhadores da faixa seguinte, de acordo com as regras da modalidade.

articles.standfirst: Rodas de conversa, palestras educativas, caminhada e oficina para profissionais de saúde estão na programação.
articles.summary: Rodas de conversa, palestras educativas, caminhada e oficina para profissionais de saúde estão na programação.
articles.body:
Uma caminhada em Rocha Leão vai integrar a programação do Setembro Amarelo — Foto: Secom

Rio das Ostras se une em defesa da vida. A campanha Setembro Amarelo, de prevenção ao suicídio, vai envolver população e profissionais de saúde do Município durante todo este mês. A programação inclui atividades educativas e de sensibilização nas unidades de saúde e uma oficina direcionada a médicos e enfermeiros da Rede.

O movimento Setembro Amarelo surgiu com a ideia de quebrar tabus, reduzir estigmas, além de estimular que as pessoas busquem e ofereçam ajuda.

Este ano, a campanha traz o tema “Escutar é estar presente”. O foco é lembrar que oferecer uma escuta acolhedora pode representar o primeiro passo para que alguém em sofrimento emocional encontre apoio e não enfrente esse momento sozinho.

A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde montou uma programação para conscientizar a comunidade, assegurar o acolhimento na Rede de Saúde, fortalecer a rede de apoio e fazer chegar a mensagem de valorização da vida a todo o Município.

ATIVIDADES – A programação se estende ao longo de todo o mês de setembro, com atividades desenvolvidas nas Unidades de Saúde da Família -USF e Unidades Básicas de Saúde – UBS.

As ações do Setembro Amarelo incluem rodas de conversa e palestras educativas (em unidades como Cantagalo, Nova Esperança, Boca da Barra, Dona Ediméia, Cláudio Ribeiro e no Âncora, com atividade direcionada à Escola Municipal Padre José Dílson Dorea).

Nas unidades de Nova Cidade, Operário, Cidade Praiana e na Clínica da Família estão previstas atividades em salas de espera e distribuição de materiais informativos.

Também estão previstas atividades fora das unidades, envolvendo as comunidades, como caminhada temática em Rocha Leão, о piquenique integrativo da USF Nilson Marins, na Praia do Abricó, e visitas domiciliares articuladas pelos Agentes Comunitários de Saúde (ACS) no Mar do Norte e Clínica da Família.

A programação contempla ainda o atendimento direcionado a adolescentes e seus acompanhantes, conduzido pelo Grupo de Psicologia e na sala de espera do Nasca – Núcleo de Atenção à Saúde da Criança e do Adolescente.

QUALIFICAÇÕES – No Dia Mundial de Prevenção ao Suicídio, 10 de setembro , a Subsecretaria de Atenção Primária promove a oficina “Transtornos mentais (ou agravos em saúde mental) mais prevalentes na APS: acolhimento, diagnóstico e conduta”, direcionada a médicos e enfermeiros da Atenção Primária.

A Secretaria de Saúde também promove, no dia 30, como parte das ações do Setembro Amarelo, o workshop “Elo de Acolhimento: o ACS e ACE na Prevenção do Suicídio”. O objetivo é preparar os Agentes Comunitários de Saúde – ACS e Agentes de Combate às Endemias – ACE a identificar pessoas em sofrimento psíquico e comportamento suicida, fortalecendo a escuta qualificada, acolhimento e encaminhamento correto de cada caso.

O workshop é realizado pela Subsecretaria de Atenção Primária à Saúde – Departamento de Estratégia de Saúde da Família, Núcleo de Vigilância às Violências e Núcleo de Educação Permanente em Saúde.

articles.title: Após crise do metanol, garrafas ganham selo que permite detectar bebidas falsificadas pelo celular | G1
articles.standfirst: Tecnologia usada em passaportes já está em cerca de 4 milhões de garrafas por mês e usa uma identificação microscópica única, analisada por IA pela câmera.
articles.summary: Tecnologia usada em passaportes já está em cerca de 4 milhões de garrafas por mês e usa uma identificação microscópica única, analisada por IA pela câmera.
articles.body:
Os casos de intoxicação por metanol registrados ao longo de 2025, que deixaram ao menos 25 mortos no país e levaram autoridades de saúde a emitir alertas , colocaram a autenticidade das bebidas no centro das discussões.

O tema, antes mais associado aos prejuízos econômicos da indústria e ao comércio ilegal, passou a envolver diretamente questões de saúde pública e fez a indústria de bebidas alcoólicas se mexer.

Nesta terça-feira (15), a Diageo, fabricante de bebidas e dona de marcas como Johnnie Walker e Smirnoff, anunciou uma solução feita em parceria com a Securetrace, empresa especializada em tecnologias de segurança usadas em documentos oficiais e sistemas de prevenção a fraudes, para verificar digitalmente a origem das bebidas da companhia.

A proposta é simples: o consumidor aponta a câmera do celular para um selo na embalagem, e o sistema informa se a garrafa foi identificada como autêntica.

O Selo Drink Seguro permite aos consumidores conferir a autenticidade de bebidas alcoólicas. — Foto: Rafaela Zem/g1

➡️ A implementação, por enquanto, está restrita ao mercado brasileiro e abrange categorias que historicamente registram casos de falsificação, como uísques, vodcas, gins, tequilas e licores.

“O selo é muito claramente para o consumidor, no sentido de resgatar a confiança, de ele conseguir ter autonomia e visibilidade daquilo que está consumindo. (...) Também é uma maneira de dar credibilidade para o estabelecimento”, afirma Paula Lindenberg, presidente da Diageo no Brasil.

Cerca de 4 milhões de garrafas já recebem o selo por mês. A tecnologia está presente em 100% do portfólio importado e na Smirnoff engarrafada no Brasil, o que corresponde a 95% do negócio de destilados da companhia no país.

Segundo a Securetrace, o selo usa a mesma tecnologia presente em recursos de proteção do passaporte brasileiro, das cédulas de euro e dos elementos holográficos da nota de R$ 100.

📎 Cada selo recebe uma espécie de impressão digital exclusiva, invisível ao consumidor , formada por padrões microscópicos que criam uma identificação única para cada unidade. Segundo a empresa, existem mais de 27 trilhões de combinações possíveis.

Quando a câmera do celular é apontada para o selo, uma inteligência artificial analisa o padrão e o compara com o banco de dados do sistema. Se houver correspondência, a autenticidade é confirmada e a plataforma exibe a mensagem "Verificado".

A tecnologia possui certificação internacional ISO 12931, norma voltada a sistemas de autenticação e combate à falsificação, explica Mario Nicoli Netto, CEO da Securetrace. Segundo a empresa, sua capacidade de impedir cópias chega a 99,99%.

"A tecnologia transforma a câmera do celular em uma ferramenta de acesso direto à origem do produto. Cada selo possui uma impressão digital única, protegida por uma tecnologia anticópia certificada internacionalmente, capaz de identificar tentativas de reprodução em segundos", afirma Mario Nicoli Netto, CEO da Securetrace.

Jovem está com suspeita de intoxicação por metanol, em Goiás — Foto: Wesley Costa/O Popular

Os episódios envolvendo metanol expuseram um dos riscos mais graves relacionados à falsificação e à adulteração de bebidas alcoólicas.

🔎 Diferentemente do etanol utilizado na produção regular de bebidas, o metanol é uma substância altamente tóxica. Sua ingestão pode causar cegueira, danos neurológicos graves, insuficiência respiratória e morte.

A crise ganhou dimensão nacional no segundo semestre de 2025. O aumento dos casos levou o governo federal a emitir alertas à população e a criar uma sala de situação para acompanhar as ocorrências.

Embora o período mais crítico tenha ficado para trás no fim daquele ano, novos episódios continuaram sendo registrados em 2026.

Uma reportagem exibida pelo Fantástico neste domingo (13) mostrou que, um ano após o início da crise , as investigações avançaram e já identificaram parte da cadeia de falsificação responsável por distribuir bebidas adulteradas .

Apesar disso, vítimas continuam convivendo com sequelas permanentes, e novos casos ainda vêm sendo registrados no país.

Embora a falsificação tenha ganhado visibilidade por causa dos riscos à saúde, ela representa apenas uma parte de um mercado ilegal muito mais amplo.

Um estudo da Euromonitor International estima que as atividades ilegais ligadas ao setor de bebidas movimentem aproximadamente R$ 28 bilhões por ano no Brasil. Nesse universo estão o contrabando, a sonegação fiscal, a produção sem registro e a falsificação.

A pesquisa aponta ainda que a falsificação representa 4,7% do mercado total de bebidas destiladas no Brasil. Apesar da parcela menor, é a prática que mais preocupa pelo risco à saúde.

Além disso, o problema gera prejuízos para fabricantes, distribuidores, varejistas e para a arrecadação pública, ao desviar recursos de impostos e alimentar estruturas clandestinas de produção e distribuição.

Por isso, o combate ao mercado ilegal tem mobilizado não apenas empresas privadas, mas também órgãos reguladores e autoridades públicas.

Chevrolet Onix ECO usa exclusivamente etanol no tanque — Foto: Divulgação / GM

O lançamento da tecnologia da Diageo ocorre em paralelo a outras iniciativas voltadas ao enfrentamento do problema. Uma das medidas em discussão é conduzida pela Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP).

Em setembro, a agência aprovou um estudo que propõe alterações na composição do etanol hidratado combustível para dificultar o desvio do produto para a fabricação clandestina de bebidas.

Entre as alternativas analisadas está a adição obrigatória de benzoato de denatônio, substância de sabor extremamente amargo, amplamente utilizada em produtos de higiene e limpeza para impedir a ingestão acidental.

A ANP também trabalha em uma medida considerada mais imediata: a inclusão obrigatória de corante verde no etanol combustível produzido pelas usinas.

A expectativa é que a mudança facilite a identificação do uso irregular do produto e reduza sua utilização em esquemas clandestinos de adulteração de bebidas.

As propostas ainda precisam passar por etapas regulatórias e avaliações técnicas, incluindo análises sobre eventuais impactos em veículos e motores.

O avanço dessas discussões mostra que o combate à fraude não depende de uma única solução.

Enquanto órgãos públicos tentam dificultar o acesso às matérias-primas utilizadas por fabricantes clandestinos, empresas investem em sistemas de autenticação, rastreamento e compartilhamento de informações com autoridades.

Ainda assim, especialistas destacam que nenhuma tecnologia é capaz de eliminar completamente a falsificação. Fiscalização, investigação policial, cooperação entre empresas e punição de grupos criminosos continuam centrais para reduzir a circulação de bebidas adulteradas.

"A preocupação de combater a falsificação é uma preocupação para sempre e é a partir daí que vem a iniciativa desse selo, com uma intenção clara de que episódios como esse nunca mais voltem a acontecer", afirma Paula Lindenberg, da Diageo.

articles.body:
Por um lado, a saúde pública brasileira é motivo de orgulho. O SUS é o maior sistema público de saúde do mundo e, de acordo com Tedros Adhanom, diretor-geral da OMS, é um exemplo para os outros países. Mas quem usa e depende do SUS sabe que a realidade impõe muitas barreiras para conseguir atendimento médico de qualidade. Um levantamento feito pelo jornal O Globo em 2025 mostra que a fila de espera para consultas dura, em média, 57 dias – isso varia de estado para estado e pode passar de 170 dias. Ardilhes detalha as propostas que os candidatos à Presidência apresentam para melhorar o atendimento básico e de especialidades no SUS, além de ideias para aumentar a cobertura vacinal e qualificar melhor a formação médica. Faz tempo que a cozinha deixou de ser um ambiente reservado apenas ao preparo das refeições. Nos projetos atuais, ela passou a integrar salas, áreas gourmet e espaços de convivência, exigindo soluções que acompanhem uma rotina cada vez mais dinâmica. Nesse cenário, os metais ganharam um papel importante ao combinar praticidade, conforto e desempenho em tarefas realizadas diariamente.

Entre as tendências que vêm conquistando espaço está a linha Farm, inspirada nas tradicionais cozinhas de fazenda, mas reinterpretada para projetos contemporâneos. Cubas amplas, torneiras de maior alcance e monocomandos facilitam o preparo dos alimentos, a higienização de utensílios e a organização da bancada, oferecendo mais liberdade de movimentos durante o uso, com acessórios práticos como dosador de sabão, tabua e lixeiras embutidas.

O desenho frontal aparente transforma a cuba em um elemento de destaque no projeto, enquanto a profundidade oferece mais conforto durante o uso.

Complementando essa proposta, o Monocomando Tera Bica Móvel reúne mobilidade, acionamento preciso e controle de temperatura em um único comando. Ergonomia, resistência dos materiais, facilidade de limpeza e durabilidade são fatores que fazem diferença em um ambiente utilizado diariamente por toda a família. articles.standfirst: Segundo meteorologistas, tendência é que o tempo siga instável nas próximas semanas. Setembro deve ter chuva acima da média para o período e volumes registrados já são históricos em algumas regiões.
articles.summary: Segundo meteorologistas, tendência é que o tempo siga instável nas próximas semanas. Setembro deve ter chuva acima da média para o período e volumes registrados já são históricos.
articles.body:
chuva tempestade temporal guarda-chuva paraná curitiba — Foto: Geraldo Bubniak/AEN

Apesar de a chuva começar a diminuir a partir desta terça-feira (15), principalmente em áreas do Sudeste, os dias de tempo instável não têm data para terminar no Centro-Sul .

Segundo os meteorologistas, a frente fria que trouxe chuva para o Sul e boa parte do Sudeste deve avançar para o norte do Espírito Santo e sul da Bahia, fazendo com que o frio siga presente nessas regiões.

Mas isso não significa que o tempo deve ficar firme nessas regiões.

"Por enquanto, está difícil de ter tempo firme no Centro-Sul do Brasil, principalmente em regiões como São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro, lugares em que o pessoal não anda mais vendo muito a cara do sol", analisa César Soares, meteorologista da Climatempo.

Segundo ele, a condição de tempo instável deve se manter porque ainda há uma circulação de ventos úmidos no mar em direção à região costeira de São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. Isso faz com que esses locais sigam com chuva fraca, garoa e também com frio.

Além disso, os temporais, que também devem dar uma trégua no Sul, devem retornar a partir de sexta-feira por conta do desenvolvimento de uma nova frente fria.

"Com isso, voltam as condições de chuva para o Sul do Brasil e, posteriormente, essa frente vai chegar ao Sudeste e também vai aumentar a nebulosidade, provocar chuva e trazer frio", prevê César.

Antes da chegada dessa nova frente fria, a tendência é que, mais para o fim da semana, as tardes se tornem mais agradáveis. Ainda assim, as máximas não devem superar os 25°C.

O meteorologista ainda destaca que, por enquanto, a volta do calor, com uma sequência de dias de tempo mais aberto, ainda está fora de cogitação , de acordo com as previsões.

O tempo instável que tem sido observado nas últimas semanas e que tende a continuar nos próximos dias é um retrato do que deve acontecer ao longo de todo o mês de setembro no Centro-Sul.

Segundo a Climatempo, a expectativa é de que o mês tenha chuvas acima da média na região . Os volumes devem ser ainda maiores do que o padrão no Paraná e em parte de São Paulo. (veja no mapa abaixo)

Boa parte do Centro-Oeste, sul e centro-oeste da Bahia, sul do Maranhão e do Piauí, Tocantins, sudeste do Pará, todo o Sudeste e grande parte do Sul também devem ter chuva acima do que normalmente é registrado no período.

Em alguns locais do país, os volumes de chuva observados nos últimos dias já são históricos.

Em São Paulo , o total de precipitação acumulado nos primeiros 14 dias do mês, de mais de 253 milímetros, é o maior desde 1943 , início das medições regulares do Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia ( Inmet ). Também é o segundo maior acumulado mensal de 2026, ficando atrás somente de janeiro.

No Rio de Janeiro , o volume registrado na primeira quinzena de setembro também é o quarto maior acumulado de chuva para o mês desde o início das medições, em 1997.

De acordo com os meteorologistas, além da sequência de frentes frias que tem avançado pelo Brasil, a atuação do El Niño , que promete ser um dos mais fortes da história , é uma das principais explicações para os temporais previstos.

Leaving Oxford without a win would deliver a dose of reality to both Tigers fans and Kiffin himself that perhaps things aren't quite as they seem, at least not yet. On the other sideline, you have an Ole Miss team that not only lost key pieces from last season, but is also being coached by a man in Pete Golding, who is entering just his sixth game as a head coach. articles.title: UK set to turn cooler as unsettled weather continues
articles.summary: As temperatures drop through the week and it starts to feel more autumnal, is it now time to put the summer clothes away?
articles.body:
Much of the UK is set to feel cooler from Tuesday, as more changeable weather moves in.

Parts of the UK are also likely to see some spells of rain, especially to northern and western parts of the UK.

The rest of the week stays a little unsettled with further spells of rain.

It could turn more settled into next week with temperatures rising above average for some, though heatwave conditions are looking increasingly unlikely.

Tuesday will start off relatively warm and muggy across central and south-eastern areas of England but further north and west it will start to feel a little cooler.

That cooler air will be moving south-east behind a cold front that will also bring a spell of rain across England and Wales for a time.

Fresher north-westerly winds will develop across all areas bringing showers - some heavy - to Scotland, Northern Ireland and more north-western parts of England and Wales.

Maximum temperatures will be around five degrees lower than Monday's values with 17 to 22C across the UK.

This is closer to the average for the time of year.

There will be a drier and brighter interlude on Wednesday, with the rest of the week staying a little unsettled with further spells of rain.

Temperatures will remain around average at 15 to 20C.

It will also start to feel a little chillier overnight with temperatures down to 8-12C - meaning those on early commutes to work or school might need to start donning extra layers.

However, while it might feel more autumnal and the right time to pack away the summer clothes, autumn - particularly September - is a fickle time.

Conditions can change with a simple switch in wind direction and we can go from chillier, autumnal weather to warmer conditions and then back again - all within a day.

Five night sky events to look out for this autumn

By Saturday, a west or south-westerly wind will bring something a little warmer with temperatures returning to above average.

With some signs of high pressure building and the prospect of drier and brighter weather, it might feel pleasantly warm for some, especially in south-eastern areas.

It is still a long way off but temperatures could rise temporarily further into next week.

The signs are, though, that a September heatwave is increasingly less likely.

articles.title: Geneva talks put Rwanda-DRC peace deal to the test
articles.summary: The talks come amid continued fighting and disputes over the implementation of key security commitments.
articles.body:
Officials from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda are due to reconvene in Geneva on September 16 and 17 for talks on the implementation of the 2025 Washington Accords.

The two-day meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) will bring together representatives of the two countries, with mediators from the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union Commission. The mechanism was established to monitor and coordinate the implementation of security commitments between the two countries.

The meeting comes as fighting continues in the eastern DRC and key commitments under the peace process remain unresolved.

The peace agreement between the DRC and Rwanda was signed in Washington, DC on June 27, 2025. The Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity, signed on December 4, reaffirmed the parties’ commitment to implementing that agreement.

Among the key security commitments are the DRC’s obligation to neutralise the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and Rwanda’s disengagement of forces and lifting of defensive measures.

The September talks will focus on whether the two sides can make further progress on those commitments.

The agreement is part of a wider diplomatic effort to end decades of conflict in the eastern DRC, a region bordering Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi that has been plagued by armed groups and repeated fighting.

The conflict has repeatedly drawn neighbouring countries into the eastern DRC. Rwanda has long said armed groups operating from DRC territory pose a threat to its security, while the Congolese government has accused Kigali of supporting armed groups seeking to seize territory and influence in the east.

“The Washington Accords reaffirm the parties’ commitment to implement the Peace Agreement between the DRC and Rwanda, agreed to in Washington, June 2025, and achieve the vision of the Regional Economic Integration Framework, to create a bold roadmap for peace, security, and unprecedented economic growth,” a US Department of State spokesperson said.

A September forecast by Security Council Report said clashes between the Congolese Armed Forces (FARDC) and the M23 armed group had continued in North and South Kivu, two provinces in the eastern DRC. It also said two central obligations under the Washington process, the neutralisation of the FDLR and Rwanda’s lifting of defensive measures, had yet to be declared complete.

Rwanda has repeatedly accused the DRC of supporting, arming and working alongside the FDLR.

The FDLR has its roots in forces and militias that fled Rwanda after the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. Some of its members were linked to the former Rwandan army and the Interahamwe militia. The group has remained active in the eastern DRC and has long been a central security concern for Rwanda.

Kinshasa, meanwhile, has accused Rwanda of supporting M23, allegations Kigali denies.

M23 first emerged as a major armed movement in 2012. After withdrawing from territory it controlled, it resurfaced in 2022 and launched a new offensive in the eastern DRC.

The group made major territorial gains in 2025, including the capture of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, and Bukavu, the capital of neighbouring South Kivu.

Although M23 is not a party to the Washington agreement, it remains central to efforts to end the wider conflict.

The US-backed process requires Rwanda and the DRC to support a separate Qatar-led dialogue between Kinshasa and M23. That process produced the Doha Framework for Peace, signed by the Congolese government and the Congo River Alliance (AFC/M23) in Doha on November 15, 2025.

The September meeting follows the sixth JSCM meeting, held in Geneva on August 12 and 13.

At that meeting, the DRC and Rwanda agreed to advance two initiatives aimed at strengthening monitoring and verification of the Washington Accords on the ground. They asked the US to consider the initiatives and provide feedback at the next JSCM meeting.

The DRC also presented its Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) plan for the FDLR and responded to questions from JSCM members.

The parties also agreed to hold a trilateral planning conference in October that will culminate in a revised operations order guiding their coordinated efforts.

The neutralisation of the FDLR is expected to remain one of the most difficult issues.

On July 28, the Congolese government said a faction of the FDLR had accepted and signed a protocol covering disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment. Kinshasa presented the move as progress towards meeting its obligations under the Washington agreement.

Rwanda rejected the move, arguing that the Washington agreement requires the FDLR to be neutralised rather than negotiated with. Kigali has also accused Kinshasa of continuing to support the group.

The disagreement matters because progress on the FDLR is tied to Rwanda’s own commitments under the Washington process.

Rwanda has maintained that its security measures along the border with the DRC are necessary to protect the country from armed groups operating in the eastern DRC. Under the Washington agreement, Rwanda is expected to disengage its forces and lift those defensive measures as part of the wider security arrangements.

For the September meeting, the FDLR issue will remain a central point of contention as the two countries try to resolve the commitments that remain at the heart of their dispute.

images.caption: The Geneva talks will test whether Rwanda and the DRC can make progress on key security commitments under their US-backed peace deal as fighting continues in the eastern DRC [Hugh Kinsella Cunningham/Getty Images]

articles.title: US confirms for first time it has deployed space weapons
articles.summary: The US Air Force Secretary says the weapons are necessary to defend the country against enemy action.
articles.body:
The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.

US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action.

Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, Meink said the US was ready for "evolving threats", but did not elaborate on the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.

Senior military leaders have previously said they planned to boost military capabilities in space, citing Russian and Chinese programmes developing ways to attack and disrupt US satellites in a future conflict.

The Trump administration has said that space-based capabilities - and interceptor missiles - are a crucial part of its planned "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US from missiles and other airborne threats.

A 1967 treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Since then, key powers including the US, Russia, and China have been exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

Last year President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the US Space Force's role in not only defending assets, but also as an attacking force.

The US Space Force - the newest branch of the US military in more than 70 years - was launched in 2019 as a way to protect American assets in space, including hundreds of satellites used for communication and surveillance.

A US Space Force spokesperson said: "Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary.

"These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands."

In early February, it was revealed that two Russian satellites have likely intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Such interceptions may have allowed Russian intelligence services to read the sensitive data they transmit, or hypothetically, even to take control of the satellites.

In 2024, the US said Russia had launched a satellite which it believed may be capable of attacking other such probes. Russia did not publicly comment on the issue.

The US Space Force says China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts".

articles.summary: US News: Pentagon's official watchdog has released the defense department's first formal accounting of US equipment and facility losses from the Iran war, deta.
articles.body: Pentagon's official watchdog has released the defense department's first formal accounting of US equipment and facility losses from the Iran war, detailing extensive damage to American military bases and diplomatic facilities across the Middle East.The special report by the defence department's inspector general, covering February 28 to June 30, said Iranian strikes “damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan”.The strikes forced US central command to “shift personnel, assets and storage facilities” as Iranian forces and their proxy groups targeted American positions, the report said.The operational changes included withdrawing Army medical evacuation helicopters from Iraq and Kuwait. As a result, “most medical evacuations have been carried out by ground … to local treatment facilities”, according to the watchdog.Bahrain attack disrupts US logisticsDamage to the US Navy's regional hub in Bahrain created “significant challenges” in establishing “adequate naval bases and support ports”, the report said. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao recently said Iran “blew the hell out of” the facility.The damage led to the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia becoming a sea logistics hub, stretching US military resupply cycles to 14-18 days, according to the report.Intermittent shortages of supplies and disruptions to the military's regional mail system further complicated operations for US sailors deployed to the Persian Gulf during the conflict.The war began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched military operations against Iran. Iran responded with missile and drone strikes against US military positions and diplomatic facilities across the region.$184 million diplomatic damageThe report, prepared with the state department and US Agency for International Development inspector general offices, estimated that Iranian attacks caused about $184 million in damage to US diplomatic facilities in the Middle East. It did not provide an estimate for damage to US military sites.In early March, two Iranian drones struck the US Embassy compound in Riyadh, causing extensive damage, including to a CIA station.A drone also targeted the US consulate in Dubai, damaging a utility building. US secretary of state Marco Rubio said at the time that it hit a “parking lot adjacent to the chancellery building”.The US Embassy in Kuwait suspended operations in March after being struck by Iranian drones and resumed emergency operations in late June.More than 600 attacks against US facilities in Iraq were recorded, a senior State Department official said in May. Those attacks caused roughly $157 million in damage.3,500 diplomatic personnel displacedUp to 3,500 diplomatic personnel were outside the region between February 23 and June 30, according to the report, as most US posts operated under authorised or ordered departure.Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE were placed under ordered departure, requiring non-emergency personnel and family members to leave.Most posts remain under “restricted operations”, with some diplomats and family members beginning to return.The report comes as US military and intelligence officials consider whether reductions in US personnel and facilities in the Middle East could become permanent after the war.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump’s mail ballot push hits Supreme Court roadblock ahead of crucial midterms
articles.summary: US News: In a major setback for US President Donald Trump, the US Supreme Court on Monday rejected his administration’s bid to impose new restrictions on mail-.
articles.body: In a major setback for US President Donald Trump, the US Supreme Court on Monday rejected his administration’s bid to impose new restrictions on mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections, allowing states to continue using their existing ballot procedures.The ruling capped a flurry of legal action just weeks before voters decide which party will control Congress. Several states have already begun sending mail ballots to voters, making a last-minute overhaul of the system particularly disruptive.The justices upheld a lower-court order blocking new requirements that the Trump administration had sought to impose through the US Postal Service (USPS). However, the decision may not be the final word on the issue, with conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicating that he could potentially side with the administration as the broader legal challenge continues.Trump’s mail ballot push hits courtsTrump signed an executive order in March directing the USPS to introduce new requirements for election-related mail, including unique barcodes on ballot envelopes and the creation of an online portal containing information about voters receiving mail ballots.The administration argued that the measures were necessary to protect election integrity and combat fraud. Trump has repeatedly criticised mail voting and has claimed, without evidence, that it can enable non-citizens to vote and is vulnerable to fraud.Twenty-three states and Washington DC challenged the order, arguing that it infringed on their constitutional authority to administer elections. They also warned that implementing the changes so close to the midterms could disrupt established voting systems and disenfranchise voters.Boston-based federal Judge Indira Talwani blocked the order on September 4, ruling that its implementation ahead of the November election could cause significant disruption. A US appeals court last week declined to suspend her order, while another federal judge, Carl Nichols, also ruled against Trump's plan on Sunday.Kavanaugh agreed that the new rules should not take effect for the 2026 elections. However, he suggested there was “at least a fair prospect” that the Postal Service could ultimately have the statutory authority to introduce them, while describing their application this year as potentially “arbitrary and capricious”.Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented, arguing that the Postal Service has broad authority to regulate mail and that the challenge to Trump's order was unlikely to succeed ultimately.States warn of election disruptionElection officials had warned that there was not enough time to implement a nationwide overhaul before the midterms. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun sending mail ballots while Trump's proposed system remained inactive.The administration's plan would have required states to use a uniform envelope format and submit voter information through an online portal, with the USPS potentially refusing to deliver ballots from states that failed to comply.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin man, woman killed by train after sitting on NYC subway tracks
articles.summary: US News: Two people of Indian-origin were fatally struck by a New York City subway train after they were seen sitting on the tracks at a Manhattan station earl.
articles.body: Two people of Indian-origin were fatally struck by a New York City subway train after they were seen sitting on the tracks at a Manhattan station early Sunday (EDT).Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul, both 24, were on the tracks at Spring Street station in downtown Manhattan shortly after 3am when a No 4 train approached, according to an incident report obtained by the New York Daily News.The train operator told supervisors that she saw the pair sitting on the tracks and tried to stop the train. The report said the woman was laughing and appeared to be pulling the man towards her when the train hit them.It was not immediately clear whether Kaul had fallen onto the tracks or climbed down, while Chitre appeared to have tried to pull him towards her, police sources told the New York Post.Video circulating on social media appeared to show the pair sitting on the tracks shortly before the collision. AmNewYork reported that the train operator activated the emergency brake but was unable to stop the train in time.Emergency responders found both victims underneath the train and pronounced them dead at the scene. Around 100 passengers were evacuated from the train after the collision, the Daily News reported.According to the Post, investigators are examining whether the pair may have been so intoxicated that they failed to realise the approaching train posed an immediate danger. No suicide notes were found, though suicide had not been ruled out as a possible motive, the newspaper reported.The two were longtime friends and had both graduated from Rutgers University in New Jersey in 2024, according to their LinkedIn profiles.The New York Police Department had not immediately provided further information to The Independent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Head down with shame': Sonam Wangchuk says LG’s compensation for Sept 24 victims small
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: A day after Ladakh Lieutenant Governor VK Saxena announced compensation for victims of the September 24 violence, in which four people were .
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A day after Ladakh Lieutenant Governor VK Saxena announced compensation for victims of the September 24 violence, in which four people were killed in alleged police firing and scores of others injured, Leh Apex Body member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk said was unhappy with the “small” compensation amount and his “head is down with shame.”In his social media post, Wangchuk on Monday evening said that “Looking at this compensation, I do not feel happy, rather my head is down with shame,” Wangchuk said.On Sunday evening the LG Ladakh said, “in our continued commitment to support the families affected by the tragic violence in Ladakh on 24 September last year, today sanctioned a compensation of Rs 15 lakh to the next of kin of each of the four deceased. An ex-gratia of Rs 3 lakh for those with major injuries and Rs 1 lakh for minor injuries has also been approved.”“While no compensation amount can replace a life lost or erase the pain endured, the Ladakh Administration firmly stands beside every affected family in their journey towards healing and overcoming the grief,” LG Ladakh said.However, Wangchuk said “you can see that the families of those who died have been offered Rs 15 lakh, while those who were injured and remain disabled for the rest of their lives are offered Rs 3 lakh.”Wangchuk said most of these people were “unarmed civilians and walking on the road” when they were fired upon. “They were shot in the head, chest and legs and that too without any firing order,” Wangchuk claimed. “There was no order to open fire, still AK-47 rifles were used against them,” he alleged.He said that the truth would have come out if the report of the inquiry commission set up to investigate the incident had been released. “Instead, that report is being suppressed. It has been a year and the truth is still not being revealed.”The LAB member said that the country must stand with Ladakh as among “those who lost their lives were former soldiers.” “During the Kargil War, some of them were injured and brought down from the mountains to hospitals. After recovering, they could have returned home but instead they chose to go back and fight for the country. Such people were shot from behind and dragged,” Wangchuk alleged“I will continue to share these stories and facts one by one if proper compensation and justice are not provided. In the interest of the nation, I have remained silent until now. But if such treatment is meted out to people who displayed such courage and sacrifice, then the truth must be placed before the country, whether or not the inquiry commission's report is ever released,” Wangchuk said.On September 24 2025, police allegedly opened fire on protesters demanding Sixth Schedule status and statehood for Ladakh after demonstrations turned violent, killing four people and injuring nearly 90. Following the violence, authorities in Leh imposed curfew-like restrictions, suspended mobile internet and arrested over 80 people with FIR registered against 87. Following the incident the Leh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance, two major political groupings refused to have talks with the centre until a judicial commission was announced.Then on October 17 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs announced a judicial probe headed by a Dr Justice B S Chauhan (former judge, Supreme Court of India) to probe into the September 24 violence in Leh making it a major outreach to the region after weeks of unrest and tension. Retired district and sessions judge Mohan Singh Parihar is its judicial secretary. The commission began its work on October 27 2025. However, the commission is yet to submit its report.After the announcement of the judicial commission, the centre held talks with representatives of the LAB and the KDA on October 22 in New Delhi. Since then Chering Dorjay Lakrook, LAB co-chairman says that LAB has raised the issue of September 24 firing and compensation for the victims in every meeting with the MHA.After the September 9, 2026 meeting in New Delhi, the Ladakh groups said the centre has assured to withdraw cases against those arrested in September 2025 and provide compensation to victims and injured.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: Meta needed data from thousands of its employees for edge in AI space, company introduced Model Capability Initiative; but then came a very 'human problem'
articles.summary: Tech News News: Meta found an internal way to get its hands on more data to strengthen its position in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. To bridge the data gap t.
articles.body: Meta found an internal way to get its hands on more data to strengthen its position in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. To bridge the data gap that didn't come from the internet, the social media giant was turning to its own employees. Meta’s elite AI unit, known as TBD, introduced the Model Capability Initiative (MCI), a programme designed to collect data on how thousands of employees use their computers.​The idea was simple: keystrokes, mouse movements and screen activity could help AI models learn how humans actually work with computers. But Meta soon ran into a very human problem: opposition from its own employees. What followed was a rebellion involving memes, flyers and a petition signed by more than 1,800 workers.​Why Meta wanted employee data​MCI was ‘invented’ by Meta because of the fundamental drawbacks that their AI systems had. Although the AI software is skilled in certain domains such as programming and research, it has not been able to perform basic computer tasks.​According to people familiar with the project, Meta believed that training AI on employee data would help the systems understand how people actually do things. MCI was conceived in TBD, an AI research lab of about 100 people, which is seen as one of Meta's most advanced AI labs.​Employees immediately pushed back​When Meta announced MCI internally in April, the response fell far short of what the company expected.​Employees raised concerns that the programme would capture sensitive information from their computers, including passwords, immigration documents and credit card details. Some also worried that the data could eventually be used to automate jobs currently performed by Meta employees.​The backlash quickly spread through internal channels. Employees shared anti-MCI memes, while the recording icon was mockingly referred to as the “Eye of Sauron”.​An internal petition opposing the programme eventually collected more than 1,800 signatures. Employees also distributed flyers at Meta offices and put up messages protesting the initiative.​At first, Meta gave workers the option to opt out for 30 minutes in June so they could do personal business. Nonetheless, activists found it insufficient and demanded that Meta cancel MCI.​Then came the data leak​However, MCI took its biggest blow toward the end of June. It emerged that data collected using the software was visible throughout Meta and even included private conversations. The leak became an instant viral sensation within Meta, seemingly confirming employees' fears about tight control of the data.​Meta subsequently switched off MCI within hours. The company said it had suspended the programme and would make it opt-in if it brought it back. Two months later, it remained suspended.​Uncertainty also remained over whether the collected data had actually been used to train Meta’s latest AI models. A manager reportedly said in July that it had not been used, while Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth told employees that the data was more useful than expected.​Get the latest technology news and updates.
